questions.q: Recording from first-hand observation means
o: drawing or photographing real objects in front of you
copying images from the internet
writing an essay
tracing a photograph
questions.why: First-hand work is valued over second-hand sources.

questions.q: Annotation in a sketchbook should
o: explain your thinking, choices and next steps
describe the weather
list materials only
be avoided
questions.why: It shows your reflection and intentions.

questions.q: Which is first-hand (primary) recording?
o: Drawing a plant you are looking at
Copying a photo from the internet
Tracing a magazine picture
Printing an artist's work
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many portfolios had little recording from primary sources, and second-hand sources were often not credited.

questions.q: A student photographs the same building at dawn, midday and dusk. What is this recording mainly useful for?
o: Proving the student visited the building
Avoiding the need to draw anything
Showing how changing light and shadow alter the forms and the mood
Making the sketchbook look full
questions.why: Recording a subject under different conditions gathers visual information (light, shadow, mood) that can feed later ideas. Photography is a valid recording method, but it should support drawing and development, not replace them.

questions.q: Why might a student make several quick, timed sketches of people moving in a busy market?
o: To capture gesture, movement and proportion quickly
To produce a finished final outcome
Because detailed drawing is not credited for recording
To avoid looking closely at the subject
questions.why: Short timed sketches train observation of moving subjects, recording gesture and proportion before the pose changes.

topics.name: Explore and select materials and techniques (AO2)

questions.q: Exploring media means
o: experimenting with different materials and techniques
using only pencil
finishing the final piece first
copying an artist exactly
questions.why: Experiments show how ideas develop.

questions.q: Studying another artist's work helps you
o: understand techniques and ideas to develop your own
copy their final piece
avoid making choices
skip research
questions.why: Contextual study informs your own direction.

questions.q: Why try several media before choosing one?
o: To fill more pages
To find which best expresses your idea and develop it further
Because the syllabus bans one medium
To copy an artist exactly
questions.why: Examiners (2023): candidates often didn't use what they discovered to move the work forward.

questions.q: Which approach best shows a student exploring a printmaking technique?
o: Printing one image once in black ink
Printing the same block on different papers and in different inks, and noting the results
Buying a ready-made print to stick in the sketchbook
Writing an essay about the history of printmaking
questions.why: Exploration means purposeful experiment: varying paper, ink and pressure and reflecting on what works. A single print or a bought one shows no investigation of the process.

questions.q: What is a resist technique in painting?
o: Painting with very thick, textured paint (impasto)
Priming a surface with gesso
Using wax or masking fluid to stop paint reaching chosen areas
Mixing sand into paint for texture
questions.why: A resist, such as wax crayon or masking fluid, repels water-based paint so those areas stay clear. The other options are different surface or texture techniques.

questions.q: Developing ideas means
o: refining compositions and solutions through a series of studies
starting a new topic each week
making one drawing
choosing at random
questions.why: Show how each step leads to the next.

questions.q: How should an artist you research be used?
o: Write their biography
Analyse how their work is made and use what you learn in your own ideas
Copy one painting as your final piece
Paste in their photo
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some gave a biography instead of researching the artwork.

questions.q: What makes annotation useful?
o: It analyses decisions and explains how the work will develop
It describes what is on the page
It lists materials only
It repeats the title
questions.why: Examiners (2023): annotations were mostly descriptive rather than analytical.

questions.q: A student's theme is 'Decay'. Which is the best way to develop ideas?
o: Make one finished painting straight away
Change the theme to something easier
Copy a famous painting of ruins as the final piece
Study rusting metal and rotting fruit, try different crops and compositions, then refine the strongest
questions.why: Development is a sequence of linked studies that test and refine ideas. Jumping to an outcome or copying skips the investigation that AO3 rewards.

questions.q: Why might a student make a small trial version, such as a maquette or colour study, before the final piece?
o: To test composition, scale or colour and solve problems before committing
Because only trial pieces are marked
So that no final outcome is needed
To copy another student's idea
questions.why: Trials let the student solve practical and visual problems in advance, so the final piece is better resolved.

questions.q: A final outcome should
o: realise your intentions and connect to your preparatory work
be unrelated to your research
be as large as possible
copy a famous work
questions.why: The journey to it is assessed too.

questions.q: What should a final piece show?
o: A new idea unrelated to the studies
A copy of an artist's work
Only technical skill
A personal response that grows clearly out of the supporting studies
questions.why: The journey from studies to outcome is assessed.

questions.q: How should a 3D piece be submitted in a portfolio?
o: Posted as the object
As a written description only
It cannot be submitted
As photographs
questions.why: Examiners (2023): photograph 3D objects and organic matter rather than sending them.

questions.q: In the Externally Set Assignment, the final outcome is made in a supervised test. What should the preparatory work have done?
o: Nothing, because only the test piece is assessed
Followed a different starting point from the test piece
Researched, developed and rehearsed the outcome so the supervised time is used well
Produced a finished copy of the outcome to trace in the test
questions.why: Preparatory work and the outcome are assessed together; good preparation means the student arrives at the test with a planned, tested idea.

questions.q: What makes a portfolio or response 'coherent'?
o: Every page explores a different, unrelated theme
Each stage links clearly to the next, showing a journey from first ideas to the outcome
All the work is in the same medium
The final outcome is the largest piece
questions.why: Coherence means the work hangs together: the outcome grows logically from the recording, exploration and development that came before.

questions.q: Complementary colours
o: sit opposite each other on the colour wheel
are next to each other
are shades of grey
are only primary colours
questions.why: e.g. red and green.

questions.q: Negative space is
o: the space around and between objects
a dark colour
a mistake
the background colour only
questions.why: Using it strengthens composition.

questions.q: Linear perspective uses
o: a horizon line and vanishing points
only colour
random lines
flat shapes
questions.why: To create the illusion of depth.

questions.q: Which describes 'tone' as a visual element?
o: The surface feel of an object
The arrangement of parts within a picture
The outline of a shape
The lightness or darkness of a colour or area
questions.why: Tone is about light and dark values, used to show form and mood. Surface feel is texture, arrangement is composition, and outline is line.

questions.q: Which art movement is known for breaking objects into geometric planes and showing several viewpoints at once?
o: Impressionism
Cubism
Pop Art
Romanticism
questions.why: Cubism, developed by Picasso and Braque, fractured forms into planes seen from multiple angles. Impressionism focused on light and colour, and Pop Art on mass culture.
